newsitem.title: GERMANY: Gaddum-banks must sell stakes to buoy bourse.
newsitem.headline: Gaddum-banks must sell stakes to buoy bourse.

text.p: Germany's stock market is not as well prepared for global competition as its bond market and banks should help by selling shareholdings, a top Bundesbank official said on Wednesday.

Risk aversion is not the only cause of German reluctance to invest in shares, Johann Wilhelm Gaddum, deputy president of Germany's central bank, said in the text of a speech due to be delivered at a stock market conference in Bonn.
An inadequate supply of attractive shares was the main cause, and banks were partly to blame because they were withholding shares from the market.

"Despite historic price highs on the stock exchange and successful share launches by various companies the mood appears to be depressed because all measures taken so far do not appear to have given the German stock market the big breakthrough."

Banks have been accused of wielding too much power through their large stakes in industrial companies. Forthcoming stock market legislation is widely expected to avoid rigorous measures like slapping a limit on banks' shareholdings.
Gaddum said that even though lawmakers, market organisers and major players had done much to prepare the share market for global competition, it still lacked breadth and depth.
The stock market could become more attractive if there were more joint stock companies and if existing share stakes were more widely distributed, he said.

"It would be desirable if banks took suitable companies public more often than they have done in the past...," Gaddum said. "This would partly deflate the recurring debate about banking power and would also contribute to strengthening and reviving the German stock market."
The lack of shares explained why trade concentrated on relatively few liquid stocks and why the share prices of medium-sized businesses often made large price swings.
A successful stock market launch of state telephone company Deutsche Telekom in November, Germany's biggest ever flotation, would help boost share ownership, Gaddum said.

But he had praise for the German system of universal banks, saying the tradition of close ties between banks and industrial companies had proved an important stabilising factor in Germany's corporate scene.
In addition, banks sometimes had good reason for buying and holding on to industrial share stakes, Gaddum said.

He also called on the government to remove differences in taxation which put partnerships and single-person companies at an advantage over incorporated firms and thereby hampered the formation of joint stock companies.
The bond market, meanwhile, was in shape for the challenge posed by European Monetary Union in 1999, when German markets would lose their main attraction the mark, Gaddum said.

Following the government's decision to issue limited volumes of short-term paper each quarter as well 30-year debt each year if possible, the market would have an adequate supply of paper across the maturity spectrum.

That would enable it to compete for investors' capital after monetary union when the absence of separate currencies will focus investors' interest on a nation's creditworthiness and debt management, Gaddum said.
He also said it was in Germany's interest to convert existing government debt into Euros from the start of the planned 1999 launch of the single currency.
Such a move would secure sufficient market liquidity for bonds and prevent a split in the market which would lead to a loss of liquidity and competitiveness, Gaddum said.
Germany has yet to decide when to transform its existing bonds into Euros.
